domain_assessment.domain: Rail-transit capital-project delivery and signal-system modernization
domain_assessment.objective: Replace an aging corridor interlocking and signal system, integrate it with PTC, maintain revenue service, and meet a federal grant-obligation deadline
domain_assessment.incident_type: Utility-strike disruption followed by cost-and-schedule risk escalation and compressed systems-integration testing

decision_points.summary: Set a 24-month baseline schedule despite contractor productivity assumptions being best-case and peer-agency reference projects taking 28 to 34 months.
evidence_before: Contractor proposal assumed efficient crew productivity using best-case numbers
Comparable peer projects typically took 28 to 34 months
Leadership pressure existed to show rapid progress against the grant
evidence_after: The project duration came to resemble the peer-project range
goals_constraints: Manage live revenue-service and possession-window constraints
alternatives: Use a schedule closer to the 28-to-34-month peer-project range
Use the contractor's 24-month proposal as the baseline
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant discounted nonidentical peer comparators and privileged the contractor's best-case proposal, adding confidence that the internal team would execute more sharply.
decision_points.time_pressure: Organizational pressure to commit to an aggressive grant-progress schedule, but no immediate deadline is described for the estimate itself.
decision_points.uncertainty: Moderate to high: peer projects were not identical, but they supplied relevant external-reference-class evidence.

decision_points.summary: Decline an updated utility survey costing about $150,000 and three weeks, proceeding with outdated maps and internal risk-management processes.
evidence_before: Utility maps were over five years old
The contractor flagged uncertainty near the bore path
evidence_after: Crews struck an unmapped high-voltage duct
The affected segment stopped for approximately two weeks
Incident response and re-sequencing costs followed
The risk register had contemporaneously rated the risk low likelihood
goals_constraints: Avoid survey cost and schedule delay
Manage uncertainty in an old corridor with incomplete utility records
alternatives: Proceed on existing maps and manage issues through normal risk-review and change-order processes
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant treated a weekly risk-review cadence and change-order process as sufficient to manage uncertainty that the survey might have reduced.
decision_points.time_pressure: The survey would add three weeks to an already aggressive project baseline.
decision_points.uncertainty: High: the physical location and condition of utilities were explicitly uncertain.

decision_points.summary: Handle a contractor risk report projecting a 12 percent cost overrun and ten-week delay through executive-summary review, delegation, and delayed escalation.
evidence_before: The contractor submitted a 40-page risk report
The report projected a 12 percent cost overrun and approximately ten weeks of schedule impact
The participant had five business days to sign off
The participant was occupied with quarterly board preparation
evidence_after: The risk picture worsened before escalation
The organization later sought a schedule accommodation from the grant side
goals_constraints: Review material within a short sign-off window
Protect grant eligibility and project schedule
alternatives: Personally review the detailed analysis, obtain a prompt readout, and escalate to the grant administrator
Read the executive summary, delegate detail review, monitor, and defer escalation
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant reports workload-driven triage and delegation, but does not clearly state avoidance of unfavorable evidence because it was threatening.
decision_points.time_pressure: High: five-business-day sign-off window combined with quarterly board preparation.
decision_points.uncertainty: Moderate: the report contained a quantified projection, but the participant expected subsequent monitoring to clarify the picture.

decision_points.summary: Compress standard eight-week systems-integration testing to five weeks to protect approximately $4 million of grant funding.
evidence_before: Six weeks remained before the grant-obligation deadline
Standard protocol called for eight weeks of testing
The engineering lead recommended the full protocol
Missing the milestone could put approximately $4 million at risk
evidence_after: Testing finished within the compressed window
The system passed and the funding deadline was met
The participant remained uncertain whether omitted verification cycles could matter later
alternatives: Request a formal extension and retain the full eight-week protocol
Compress testing to five weeks by removing redundant verification cycles
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant says that avoiding loss of the $4 million was the decisive consideration, despite accepting a sound engineering case for the full protocol.
decision_points.time_pressure: High: six weeks remained against an eight-week standard testing protocol.
decision_points.uncertainty: Moderate: the future reliability consequence of trimmed verification was unknown at the time of reflection.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “The contractor's proposal assumed pretty efficient crew productivity — their best-case numbers.” “We went with 24 months. I figured our team was sharper on execution than what those other durations reflected.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Baseline-schedule discussion, following the interviewer question about contractor numbers versus peer projects.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant uses an optimistic, project-specific forecast based on best-case contractor productivity while discounting an available external reference class of comparable projects. The added belief that this team would execute better supports an overly favorable duration estimate rather than a merely technical adjustment for project differences.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The peer projects were not identical in vendor and corridor configuration, so some adjustment to their duration range was justified. However, the combination of best-case assumptions, a substantially shorter estimate, and later convergence toward the reference class makes a purely justified adjustment less persuasive.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: None for a defensible occurrence; a contemporaneous contingency analysis would further distinguish the estimate from a reasoned aggressive target.

revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the current contrast between the contractor's best-case productivity assumptions, the 28-to-34-month reference class, and the selected 24-month schedule.
preserve: The distinction between nonidentical peer projects and nonetheless relevant reference-class evidence
The later observation that actual productivity resembled peer-project performance
The absence of an explicit bias label
avoid_creating: A second planning-fallacy occurrence in later schedule revisions

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “We have a solid weekly risk-review cadence, and a change-order tracking process that's pretty tight. I felt like if something came up, we'd catch it fast and deal with it through that mechanism rather than paying upfront to eliminate the uncertainty.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Utility-survey decision, in response to the question about what tipped the choice toward proceeding without a survey.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant substitutes confidence in detection-and-response processes for reduction of the underlying external physical uncertainty. Weekly reviews and change-order tracking may improve response after discovery, but they do not establish that an unmapped high-voltage duct can be controlled or prevented.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The participant may have made a legitimate cost-benefit choice to accept and manage a low-probability risk. The occurrence remains supported because the stated rationale specifically treats internal oversight as a functional substitute for eliminating uncertainty, rather than solely as a contingency measure.

revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the distinction between managing an issue after it appears and obtaining information intended to reduce uncertainty before construction.
preserve: Survey cost and three-week schedule implication
avoid_creating: A second illusion-of-control cue in the risk-report decision
An explicit statement that the process guarantees prevention

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “In hindsight it feels almost obvious — that corridor's old, the utility ownership records were a mess, of course something was going to be down there that we didn't know about.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Post-outcome reflection on the utility strike, immediately followed by confirmation that the contemporaneous risk register rated the risk low likelihood.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: After the outcome, the participant reconstructs the utility conflict as nearly inevitable or obvious. This retrospective certainty conflicts with the documented contemporaneous assessment that the likelihood was low, supporting a post-outcome shift in perceived foreseeability.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Learning after the incident may have revealed genuinely new facts about utility ownership records or corridor conditions. The text nevertheless uses broad pre-existing facts—old corridor and disordered records—to characterize the event as obvious, while the contemporaneous risk rating establishes a useful contrast.

revision.location: Decision point 2, reflective probe after the utility-strike outcome.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the explicit temporal distinction between post-outcome reflection and the contemporaneous low-likelihood risk-register rating.
preserve: The separate in-the-moment control belief supporting cb_02
avoid_creating: A second retrospective certainty claim at another decision point
An implication that the strike was technically certain rather than perceived as obvious after the fact

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “I read the executive summary, delegated the detailed analysis to one of my leads, and told the team to keep monitoring things as they came in.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Risk-report handling discussion, after the participant describes being occupied with quarterly board preparation.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The conduct is compatible with reduced engagement with adverse information, but the text does not establish that the participant avoided the report because the projected cost and schedule news was aversive. Delegation under a five-day deadline and competing board work is also a credible managerial triage response.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The participant had a substantial report, only five business days for sign-off, and a concurrent board-preparation obligation. Delegating technical review to a lead and waiting for updated monitoring could be ordinary workload management or reliance on appropriate staff expertise.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: A subtle indication that the unfavorable projection itself motivated deferral, selective review, or avoidance of escalation; the evidence should distinguish this from delegation with an active follow-up plan.

revision.location: Decision point 3, participant response beginning “I read the executive summary...”
revision.current_defect: The response demonstrates incomplete review and delayed escalation but not threat-motivated avoidance of unfavorable information. Current evidence supports workload triage at least as well as an Ostrich Effect mechanism.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Add one restrained sentence showing that the adverse projection motivated deferral, for example: after noting the 12 percent and ten-week figures, have the participant say that the figures were bad enough that they did not want to take the detailed report to grants until the next monitoring update might clarify or soften the picture. Retain the delegation to the lead, but specify that the participant did not request a detailed readout or initiate escalation during the sign-off window.
preserve: The 12 percent cost-overrun and ten-week schedule-impact estimates
The later escalation and accommodation request
avoid_creating: An explicit textbook claim such as “I avoided bad news”
A second omission-based bias at the utility-survey decision
A new factual claim that the report was inaccurate or intentionally misleading

target_occurrence_audit.bias: Loss Aversion or Loss Framing effect
target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “We couldn't afford to lose that $4 million. That was really the driver.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Testing-compression decision, in response to the interviewer question about how the participant selected the five-week protocol.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The decision is explicitly framed around avoiding loss of already expected grant funding. However, the text does not establish that this loss framing caused asymmetric weighting relative to an economically equivalent gain or to the safety and reliability value of completing the full protocol.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Protecting approximately $4 million of funding under a hard deadline can be a rational organizational priority. The engineering lead's recommendation was acknowledged as sound, and the participant did not assert that safety concerns were irrelevant; the system also passed, though that later outcome cannot validate the prior decision.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: Evidence that preserving an already committed $4 million was psychologically or evaluatively weighted differently from obtaining an equivalent upside, rather than simply being a rational response to a material funding exposure.

revision.location: Decision point 4, immediately after the participant explains that they could not afford to lose $4 million.
revision.current_defect: The current text demonstrates loss-framed language but cannot distinguish a framing effect from a justified funding-versus-protocol tradeoff.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Insert one brief equivalence probe and response without changing the actual event: ask whether the participant would have compressed testing if full funding were secure but finishing by the deadline created an additional $4 million upside. Have the participant answer that they probably would have retained the full protocol because protecting money already committed felt materially different from pursuing the same amount as an upside.
preserve: The engineering lead's sound full-protocol recommendation
The unresolved long-run relevance of omitted verification cycles
avoid_creating: A claim that safety or reliability does not matter
A new factual change to grant terms, testing results, or the actual decision
A second loss-aversion episode elsewhere in the interview

bias_level_counts.bias: Loss Aversion or Loss Framing effect

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “I figured our team was sharper on execution than what those other durations reflected.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The participant expresses an unsupported favorable comparative judgment about the team's execution ability relative to peer agencies.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The participant may possess unreported evidence about team capability, contractor capacity, or corridor-specific conditions. The statement also operates as part of the same evidence-weighting episode already required for Planning Fallacy, so it should not be separately counted.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “The peer projects weren't identical setups ... so I didn't think the comparison held up perfectly. We went with 24 months.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: Relevant external-reference-class information was discounted in favor of a project-specific forecast.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Differences in signal vendor and corridor configuration can legitimately reduce peer-project comparability. This is best treated as the evidence mechanism of the supported Planning Fallacy occurrence, not as an accidental independent bias.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “I didn't loop in the grant administrator or escalate it up the chain at that point — I figured we'd get a clearer picture once the monitoring caught up.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: Potential postponement of escalation following unfavorable risk information.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The stated reason is uncertainty pending additional monitoring, not concern about reputational, political, or personal consequences of escalation. It is not independently distinguishable from the weak intended Ostrich-Effect episode.

nonbias_cues.cue: The project later resembled the 28-to-34-month duration range of peer agencies.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: An unfavorable later outcome does not itself establish Planning Fallacy. The supported occurrence rests on the earlier use of best-case assumptions and discounting of reference-class data, not on the schedule result.

nonbias_cues.cue: The utility risk was recorded as low likelihood.
nonbias_cues.location: Risk-register discussion after the utility strike.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: A low-likelihood rating can be a reasonable but incorrect risk judgment. It becomes relevant to Hindsight Bias only because it conflicts with the participant's later assertion that the strike was almost obvious.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant delegated detailed report review while preparing quarterly board material.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Delegation, workload, and time pressure are ordinary organizational conditions. They support Ostrich Effect only if the text establishes that unfavorable information, rather than workload alone, motivated avoidance.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant prioritized a $4 million grant exposure over full testing protocol.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: A financially consequential loss under a hard deadline may justify a difficult tradeoff. Loss aversion requires evidence of asymmetric valuation caused by loss framing, not merely a decision to protect valuable funding.

nonbias_cues.cue: The system passed commissioning within the compressed testing window.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: A favorable short-term outcome neither proves the earlier testing decision was unbiased nor proves that omitted verification cycles are immaterial.

causal_claims.claim: Proceeding without an updated utility survey left the project exposed to unidentified underground infrastructure and was followed by a high-voltage-duct strike.
causal_claims.assessment: Plausible contributory causal account, but not proven. The interview establishes outdated maps and contractor-flagged uncertainty, but does not establish that the specific survey would certainly have identified the duct or prevented the strike.

causal_claims.claim: Delayed detailed engagement and escalation after the contractor's risk report allowed the risk picture to worsen before it was brought into focus.
causal_claims.assessment: Chronologically plausible but causally under-specified. The text does not identify what specific mitigation would have been available or whether earlier escalation would have reduced cost or schedule impact.

causal_claims.claim: Compressing testing protected grant funding while possibly increasing unresolved future reliability risk.
causal_claims.assessment: The funding outcome is directly stated. The future reliability implication remains appropriately uncertain and should not be represented as established harm.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Treating the utility strike as proof that the omitted survey would have detected the duct.
correlation_causation_risks.mitigation: Use conditional language: the survey could have reduced uncertainty or increased detection probability, rather than asserting prevention.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Treating later schedule deterioration as proof that delegation caused the full deterioration.
correlation_causation_risks.mitigation: Separate delayed escalation from other possible drivers, including actual utility conditions, contractor performance, and grant-administration response.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Treating successful commissioning as evidence that compressed verification was safe or equivalent to the full protocol.
correlation_causation_risks.mitigation: Retain the participant's uncertainty about downstream implications.

causal_audit.changed_variable: Whether an updated utility/geotechnical survey is commissioned before the fixed-price baseline is finalized versus the participant proceeding without it and relying on existing risk-management processes.
held_constant: Grant obligation deadline and approximately $4 million funding exposure
Contractor identity and fixed-price contract structure
Participant role, authority, and team composition
Corridor location and aging utility environment
Occurrence and timing of the utility strike, as specified in the hidden test plan
causal_audit.explanation: The interview preserves the central survey-versus-no-survey decision and keeps the major project conditions stable. However, the explicit hypothetical asks what would happen with unlimited time and budget, which changes two decision constraints rather than isolating survey commissioning alone. The interview also should not imply that survey commissioning deterministically prevents the utility strike. The counterfactual is usable for contextual reflection but is not a clean causal test as currently elicited.

global_revision_constraints: Retain exactly four decision points and the existing chronology.
Do not treat the later utility strike, later schedule slippage, or successful commissioning as proof of bias.
Keep Planning Fallacy at baseline setting, Illusion of Control at the survey choice, and Hindsight Bias only in the later reflection on the utility outcome.
Repair Ostrich Effect at the risk-report episode through threat-motivated information avoidance, not by adding generic overload or a second control belief.
Repair Loss Aversion through an equivalent gain-versus-loss probe, not by intensifying the real financial stakes or portraying safety as unimportant.
Do not add a claim that the survey would certainly have found the high-voltage duct or prevented the strike.
Do not introduce new decision points, new organizational actors, or altered grant terms.
revision_order: Revise cb_04 by adding a restrained adverse-information-avoidance cue within the existing report-review response.
Revise cb_05 by adding a concise equivalent-gain probe and participant response after the existing testing rationale.
Retain cb_01, cb_02, and cb_03 without substantive changes.
Recheck that the revised report-handling and testing episodes remain separate and do not create accidental additional manifestations.

failure_flags.detail: Current report-handling behavior is equally or more plausibly explained by time pressure, delegation, and ordinary uncertainty management than by avoidance of unfavorable information.
Loss-framed wording is present, but the interview does not demonstrate asymmetric weighting caused by framing rather than a rational response to a $4 million funding exposure.
The explicit unlimited-time-and-budget hypothetical changes more than survey commissioning and therefore does not cleanly isolate the intended counterfactual variable.
